identification.summary: Webworm is the name Symantec uses for a cyberespionage group active since at least 2017 that targets government agencies and enterprises in IT services, aerospace and electric power across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia and other Asian countries [S1]. Symantec reported in September 2022 that the group had built modified versions of three older RATs (Trochilus, Gh0st RAT and 9002 RAT) [S1]. ESET, which describes Webworm as China-aligned, reported in May 2026 that the group had expanded into Europe and added the Discord-based EchoCreep and Microsoft Graph-based GraphWorm backdoors in 2025 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Symantec tied Webworm to Space Pirates (documented by Positive Technologies in 2022), said the two may be the same group, and cautioned that shared tooling makes attribution difficult [S1]. Press coverage of Positive Technologies' later work also links Space Pirates to Webworm [S3]. ESET reports Webworm overlaps with the clusters FishMonger (Aquatic Panda), SixLittleMonkeys and Space Pirates [S7]. One search-result summary of Help Net Security coverage lists UAT-8302 as another name, but the Cisco Talos UAT-8302 coverage seen does not mention Webworm, so the link is unverified [S8]. Positive Technologies' dating of Space Pirates differs from Symantec's (late 2019 vs 2017 per coverage), so start dates are disputed [S3]. This record has no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID.

attribution.sponsor: No government attribution found in the sources gathered. ESET describes Webworm as China-aligned [S4][S6]. Symantec describes the group as a cyberespionage actor and does not name a sponsor in the coverage seen [S1].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. ESET attributes its 2025 findings to Webworm after decrypting EchoCreep Discord messages and finding a SoftEther VPN configuration whose IP address matched infrastructure previously linked to the group [S4][S5]. Symantec cautions that shared older tools make attribution difficult [S1].
attribution.basis: Tooling (modified Trochilus, Gh0st RAT, 9002 RAT, McRat, custom proxies) and infrastructure overlap per Symantec and ESET [S1][S4][S5]. Positive Technologies states Deed RAT has been exclusive to Space Pirates to date and shares code with ShadowPad [S3]. Symantec noted the older RATs are associated with Chinese APT groups such as APT10 and APT31 [S1].

objectives: Cyberespionage against government, IT services, aerospace and electric power targets [S1]. ESET reports exfiltration of files from a government organization in Spain between December 2025 and January 2026 [S5].

regions: Russia, Georgia, Mongolia and other Asian countries (2022 reporting) [S1]
Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia and Spain (2025) [S4][S5]
targeting.notes: ESET says the group initially focused on Asia and has expanded to Europe [S4][S7]. Space Pirates, which Symantec links to Webworm, was reported by Positive Technologies to hit at least 16 organizations in Russia and Serbia (counts vary by outlet) across government, education, security, aerospace, agriculture, defense, energy and healthcare [S3]. ESET reports an attacker-operated server used for reconnaissance against more than 50 unique targets [S5].

capabilities.summary: Symantec describes initial access through social engineering with decoy documents and droppers that load modified Trochilus, Gh0st RAT and 9002 RAT, with most changes aimed at evading detection [S1]. Other tools Symantec lists include Zupdax, Deed RAT, BH_A006 (a modified Gh0st RAT) and MyKLoadClient [S1]. Positive Technologies reports Deed RAT is exclusive to Space Pirates and shares code with ShadowPad [S3]. ESET reports a shift over about two years from traditional backdoors toward (semi-)legitimate utilities such as SOCKS proxies and SoftEther VPN, plus custom proxies WormFrp, ChainWorm, SmuxProxy and WormSocket, and suspects the group may be building a hidden network from compromised systems [S6][S7]. In 2025 it added EchoCreep (Discord C2: file transfer, runtime reports, command execution) and GraphWorm (Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive for tasking and exfiltration, with a separate directory per victim) [S4][S5][S6]. It staged tools on a GitHub repository impersonating a WordPress fork [S4]. The initial access method for the 2025 backdoors is unknown [S7].

campaigns.name: Space Pirates disclosure (Russian aerospace)
campaigns.summary: Positive Technologies first publicly documented Space Pirates attacking Russia's aerospace sector. Symantec later linked this group to Webworm [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Modified legacy RATs
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported Webworm using modified Trochilus, Gh0st RAT and 9002 RAT against government and enterprise targets in Russia, Georgia, Mongolia and other Asian countries. Some indicators appeared to be in testing or pre-deployment [S1].

campaigns.name: Space Pirates Deed RAT campaign
campaigns.summary: Positive Technologies reported attacks on at least 16 organizations in Russia and Serbia (counts vary: Dark Reading cites 17 victims), with heavier use of Deed RAT [S3].

campaigns.name: Earliest EchoCreep Discord commands
campaigns.summary: ESET found the earliest commands in the EchoCreep Discord channel dated 21 March 2024. Proxy tools and SoftEther VPN were mainly seen in 2024 [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: European government and South African university campaign
campaigns.summary: ESET observed Webworm targeting government organizations in Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia and Spain and a South African university, using EchoCreep, GraphWorm and custom proxies [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Spain government exfiltration
campaigns.summary: Between December 2025 and January 2026 operators uploaded 20 new files to the C2 service, two exfiltrated from a Spanish government organization [S5].

campaigns.name: ESET publication
campaigns.summary: ESET published its research on Webworm's expanded arsenal and European targeting [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: China-aligned cyberespionage group per ESET, active since at least 2017 per Symantec, overlapping with Space Pirates [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Modified legacy RATs, Deed RAT, EchoCreep, GraphWorm, custom proxies and SoftEther VPN [S1][S3][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Discord channels and Microsoft OneDrive used as C2, SoftEther VPN, a GitHub repository impersonating a WordPress fork used for staging, and possible compromised-host proxy network [S4][S6].
diamond.victim: Government, IT services, aerospace, electric power and a university across Asia, Russia, Europe and South Africa [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting of Russian, Georgian, Mongolian and European governments is consistent with government and strategic espionage, but no source here states tasking [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Abuse of legitimate cloud and messaging services (Discord, Microsoft Graph, OneDrive) for C2 that blends with normal traffic [S5][S6].

gaps: No government attribution or named sponsor in the sources gathered; 'China-aligned' is ESET's characterization.
Initial access method for the 2025 EchoCreep and GraphWorm intrusions is unknown [S7].
Whether Webworm, Space Pirates and UAT-8302 are one cluster is unverified; Symantec says they may be the same, and the Talos UAT-8302 coverage seen does not mention Webworm [S1][S8].

Primary documents (Symantec blog, Positive Technologies reports, ESET WeLiveSecurity article) could not be opened with WebFetch in this environment; claims rest on search-result summaries and trade coverage. Verify details against originals.

A claim that Solar (Rostelecom) tracks a 2025 campaign against Russian IT firms with LuckyStrike Agent under the name Erudite Mogwai appeared only in a search summary and was not verified, so it is excluded.
Dates differ between sources on the span of the ESET research (early 2024 to early 2025 per Dark Reading; 2025 activity per May 2026 coverage) [S4][S7].
No MITRE group ID or Microsoft name is recorded for Webworm.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government networks, aerospace and energy-sector IT service providers, and the cloud tenants they use (Microsoft OneDrive and Graph, Discord reachability) are relevant terrain; the group has moved from Asia to European governments [S1][S4]. STEP 2: The adversary blends C2 into legitimate cloud services and uses proxy and VPN tooling (SoftEther, WormFrp, ChainWorm) that may turn compromised hosts into relays [S5][S6]. STEP 3: Observed template is a social-engineering lure or an unknown access vector, then a loader and RAT or cloud-C2 backdoor, then proxy tooling and file exfiltration [S1][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against European and Asian government and aerospace targets using cloud-service C2. MDCOA is use of compromised allied or partner hosts as proxy infrastructure to stage access toward higher-value networks, which ESET suspects is a goal [S6]. Candidate indicators: Discord traffic from servers or government workstations, unexpected Microsoft Graph or OneDrive API calls from non-standard processes, SoftEther VPN binaries or configs, and repositories impersonating legitimate software forks [S4][S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting on Webworm, Space Pirates and overlap clusters (FishMonger, SixLittleMonkeys) and treat them as possibly related until separated [S1][S7]. (2) Authorities: hunting for cloud-service C2 on partner or allied networks depends on host-nation and tenant-owner consent; coordinate before acting on coalition systems. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize egress monitoring and application allowlisting for Discord and Graph API use on sensitive enclaves, and review contractor and IT-service-provider connections [S1][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs in countries ESET names (Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia, Spain) [S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Space Pirates is a cybercrime group that has been active since at least 2017. They primarily target Russian companies and have been observed using various malware, including Deed RAT and ShadowPad. The group uses a combination of publicly available tools and their own protocols to communicate with their command-and-control servers.
